title: CO2 laser cutter: take the motors, rails, pumps and optics; leave the tube supply alone
summary: A CO2 laser cutter gives you stepper motors, linear rails and belts, a water pump, an air pump, an exhaust blower, a 24 V supply, three mirrors and a focus lens, in about an hour. Two things can kill or blind you: the tube's 20–30 kV power supply, which can hold a charge after unplugging, and the invisible beam. Never power the machine with it open.

steps.text: Make sure it can never fire while you work. Pull the plug from the wall and from the machine and take the key out. Unplug the water pump, the air pump and the exhaust blower too. Don't reconnect power to any part of this machine while the lid is open or an interlock switch is bridged, even to test a motor.
steps.warn: The beam is infrared and invisible. A short exposure to the beam or to a reflection from a shiny part can blind you, burn skin and start fires. Never run it open.

steps.text: Open the electronics bay and the cutting area, wearing gloves: honeycomb beds and burnt residue are sharp and dirty. Photograph the wiring and label what you will unplug. With a meter, prove the mains terminals and the 24 V supply output are dead. Wait at least 10 minutes after unplugging.
steps.warn: The tube's power supply can hold a charge of tens of kilovolts even after it is unplugged. Keep every part of you away from its output wire and the tube's HV terminal until step 3 is done.

steps.text: Earth the high-voltage side before you reach near it. Make an earth stick: a dry wooden or plastic rod at least 60 cm long, a screwdriver or bare metal tip taped to its end, and a thick flexible wire from the tip to a clip. Clip the wire to bare metal on the frame first. With your free hand in your pocket and standing on a dry floor, touch the tip to the tube's HV terminal (under the silicone boot on the thick wire), then to the supply's HV output, and hold each for 30 seconds. Leave the earth wire clipped on for the rest of the job.
steps.warn: The resistor tool in safety_discharge_capacitor is made for a few kilovolts and can flash over at 20–30 kV. Use a plain earth stick, keep 30 cm or more from the terminal, and never touch the terminal with your hand.

steps.text: Drain the water. Lift the coolant hoses off the tube over a bucket, then the pump hoses, and empty the tube jacket, the hoses and the bucket or chiller tank. Take out the pump with its cord and the flow switch if there is one. Mop up spills at once.
steps.warn: Water near the supply and mains wiring is a shock risk. Mop up spills before you go on.

steps.text: Decide whether to take the glass tube. It is 0.7–1.5 m of thin glass with water fittings at each end and has no use outside a laser cutter, so most people leave it in. To take it, keep the earth clip on the HV end, undo the cradle clamps, lift it with both hands at both ends and pack it in a padded box.
steps.warn: If it breaks, the slivers are sharp and the water is dirty. Wear eye protection. Never lift it by its cables or by one end.

steps.text: Remove the mirrors and the lens. There are usually 3 small mirrors in adjustable mounts at the corners of the beam path, and the lens sits in the laser head's focus tube (unscrew the nozzle and tip the lens out into your gloved hand). Handle by the edges, wrap each in soft cloth or lens tissue and keep them in a closed box. Don't wipe them; blow off dust.
steps.warn: The lens is zinc selenide. Whole, it is safe to hold; broken or ground up, its dust is poisonous. Don't sand, scrape or heat optics. If one breaks, wear gloves and a mask, pick the pieces up with damp tissue, bag them and wash your hands.

steps.text: If the machine has a red pointer (a small red laser module near the head or beam combiner), unplug it and take it with its wires. It is under 5 mW but can still hurt an eye. Never look into it, and power it only from a source of the right voltage (often 3–5 V) when you are ready to test it.

Take the pumps and blower. Unplug and unscrew the air-assist pump (a small diaphragm pump on the back or underside), the exhaust blower from its duct and the cooling fans. Keep each mains lead, cut near the machine and not near the motor, and note the label volts and watts. Spin each blower by hand: it should turn freely.

Take the motion system. Support the gantry (the cross beam that carries the head) with one hand. Unclamp the belts, unscrew the stepper motors (4 screws each), slide the carriages with their wheels or bearings off the rails, and unbolt the rails. Keep belts, pulleys, wheels and bearings with their screws. On bigger machines the bed lift has a motor and screws: take them too.

Take the 24 V supply, the controller and stepper driver boards, the homing sensors, the lid interlock switches and the wiring harness. Unplug rather than cut where you can. Leave the laser power supply (the metal box with the thick HV wire) where it is, closed, with its HV output still earthed.
steps.warn: Don't open the laser power supply or try to test it. Even unplugged, treat it as live.

steps.text: Bag the small parts by type. Wet-wipe the parts and wash your hands: residue from cut plastics and wood is oily and can be toxic. Keep the optics and pointer in a closed, labelled box away from children.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Stepper motors.** Two or three NEMA 17 or 23 motors, usually run from 24 V. Drive them from stepper driver modules (see teardown_cnc_router for sorting their wires).
- **Rails, wheels, bearings, belts and pulleys.** Parts for a plotter, a small mill or a printer, or any straight-line motion.
- **Mirrors.** Polished discs of silicon, molybdenum or coated metal, about 20–25 mm across. Use them as signal mirrors, or to reflect sunlight into a solar cooker.
- **Focus lens.** A clear zinc selenide lens of about 50 mm focal length. It focuses sunlight to a hot spot that lights tinder. Never look through it at the sun.
- **Red pointer.** A small red laser. Keep it for alignment work, and only with a current-limited driver.
- **Coolant pump.** A mains submersible pump of 20–80 W for a shower, a solar water heater, a fountain or irrigation.
- **Air-assist pump.** A 20–135 W diaphragm pump that aerates water or gives a little air for a small forge.
- **Exhaust blower.** A 50–400 W centrifugal fan: ventilation, a forge blower or a fume extractor.
- **24 V supply.** 5–15 A, enough for LED lighting, a 24 V pump or a small winch.

## The tube and its supply: leave them

- The tube is a fragile glass tube filled with a mixture of gases (CO2, nitrogen, helium). It is no use without its supply.
- The supply turns mains into 20–30 kV and can deliver a lethal current. Taking it out is only for someone who knows why they want it. If you must, don't open the case, keep its output earthed with the clip lead, and store and carry it that way. Never power it outside the machine.

## Variations

- Small desktop machines (K40 style) have an open interior; larger ones have 60–150 W tubes and a separate chiller. A chiller holds refrigerant: leave its loop sealed (see safety_refrigerant).
- Sealed metal-tube CO2 lasers are RF powered and have no kilovolt supply, but the same invisible beam.
- Diode engravers and fibre markers are different machines. Diode lasers and fibre lasers are also dangerous to the eyes (see the laser hazard).

## What to leave

- The tube and its power supply.
- The controller, if its firmware is locked to the machine.
